paragraphs: Strong average performance on a collection of games can hide serious weaknesses on individual games. This paper addresses that problem in the Atari benchmark, where earlier reinforcement learning agents could excel at many games while struggling badly with others. Its goal is broad competence across the entire set of 57 games, including the challenging cases that averages can obscure.

Agent57 uses a neural network to represent a family of policies with different priorities. Some emphasize exploration, while others concentrate on exploiting what the agent has already learned. An adaptive mechanism decides which policy should receive priority during training. The authors also introduce an architectural parameterization intended to make learning more consistent and stable.

The reported result is an agent that exceeds the standard human benchmark on every one of the 57 games, which the authors identify as a first for deep reinforcement learning. The significance is coverage across this benchmark: adapting exploration priorities helps address uneven performance across games. The comparison concerns the specified human benchmark, rather than every possible measure of human playing ability.
icml-2020-agent57-outperforming-the-atar.tldr: Agent57 adaptively prioritizes exploratory and exploitative policies to exceed the standard human benchmark on all 57 Atari games.

paragraphs: The geometry used to represent a graph can influence which patterns a learning system captures naturally. Hyperbolic and spherical spaces offer useful biases for structures such as hierarchies and cycles. This paper extends graph convolutional networks beyond ordinary Euclidean geometry, allowing their representations and operations to live in constant curvature spaces and combinations of those spaces.

The construction has two main ingredients. A unified mathematical description allows differentiable movement between negative, zero, and positive curvature. Gyro-barycentric coordinates supply a generalization of the familiar center of mass, supporting the aggregation operations needed by graph networks. As curvature approaches zero from either direction, the resulting models smoothly recover their Euclidean counterparts.

Experiments show improvements over Euclidean graph convolutional networks on node classification and distortion minimization for symbolic data whose discrete curvature indicates non-Euclidean behavior. These findings support matching representation geometry to the structure of the data in the evaluated settings. The contribution also makes these geometries part of a connected model family, rather than treating each geometry as an unrelated architecture.
icml-2020-constant-curvature-graph-convo.tldr: The paper generalizes graph convolutional networks across constant curvature geometries and reports gains on data exhibiting non-Euclidean structure.

paragraphs: Clustering on a road network or another weighted graph uses shortest-path distances rather than ordinary straight-line distances. This paper studies how to compress such clustering problems using a coreset: a small summary that approximately preserves the clustering objective for every possible choice of centers. Preserving all center choices makes the summary useful throughout the search for a good clustering.

For graph k-Median, the authors construct a coreset in near-linear time. With the accuracy requirement and number of centers fixed, its size grows linearly with the graph's treewidth. A nearly matching lower bound shows that the size dependence is close to unavoidable. The key technical step bounds a complexity measure called shattering dimension by treewidth, uniformly over point weights.

On real road networks, the method produces very small coresets with high accuracy and substantially speeds up existing approximation algorithms, including local search. The theoretical result connects compressibility to graph structure, while the experiments show how that compression can translate into faster clustering. Coresets also provide a route to reducing storage and communication requirements.
icml-2020-coresets-for-clustering-in-gra.tldr: Graph k-Median coresets can be constructed in near-linear time with size controlled by treewidth, yielding substantial clustering speedups on road networks.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can reduce a model's accuracy, but identifying those mistakes is itself difficult. This paper investigates a simple filtering approach that uses a preliminary trained model to help locate mislabeled examples. The central idea is to examine neighborhoods in a representation produced by that model, making the model part of the process for improving its training data.

The method applies k-nearest neighbors to the preliminary model's logit layer, the layer containing its prediction scores. This supplies a space in which examples can be compared for filtering. The paper studies whether this neighborhood-based procedure can remove incorrectly labeled training data and thereby support more accurate models. Its focus is a straightforward data-filtering step built around an existing model representation.

The empirical study reports that this approach removes mislabeled examples and produces more accurate models than many recently proposed methods. The authors also provide new statistical guarantees supporting its efficacy. Together, these contributions give both empirical and theoretical support for the filtering strategy, while the comparative accuracy claim remains a finding of the reported study.
icml-2020-deep-k-nn-for-noisy-labels-d05.tldr: Nearest-neighbor filtering in a preliminary model's logit space can remove mislabeled training examples and improve accuracy.

paragraphs: Online allocation requires deciding how to spend limited resources as requests arrive, without knowing future demand. Each action earns revenue and consumes resources. This paper considers concave revenue functions and assumes that requests' revenue and consumption characteristics are drawn independently from an unknown probability distribution. The objective is to maximize total revenue while respecting the overall resource budget.

The algorithms maintain a dual multiplier for each resource, which acts as a price reflecting its use in allocation decisions. These multipliers are updated through online mirror descent. Different choices of the method's reference function recover dual subgradient descent and dual exponential weights, placing several update strategies within one general framework.

The authors prove sublinear expected regret relative to the best allocation chosen with hindsight. They also establish the optimal order of regret when the time horizon and initial resource quantities grow proportionally. These guarantees connect simple resource-price updates to long-run allocation quality under the stated stochastic assumptions. Applications discussed include budget-constrained bidding in repeated auctions and online proportional matching with high entropy.
icml-2020-dual-mirror-descent-for-online.tldr: Updating resource prices with dual mirror descent gives efficient online allocation algorithms with optimal-order regret under the stated stochastic scaling conditions.

paragraphs: Web applications involving millions of users and thousands of items can lead to linear programs with enormous numbers of variables and constraints. Although these formulations express the optimization problem directly, their scale makes them difficult for existing solvers. The paper also notes that ad hoc decompositions used to handle such problems offer limited optimality guarantees and can produce suboptimal results.

ECLIPSE addresses scale with a distributed algorithm for a perturbed version of the linear program. It applies gradient-based optimization to the smooth dual of that perturbed problem. The main computations are matrix-vector multiplications distributed across machines, with load balancing, and efficient distributed projection operations. This formulation organizes the optimization around operations suitable for distributed execution.

Experiments on real-world data demonstrate problems containing one trillion decision variables, beyond the capabilities of the existing solvers described in the paper. The result establishes the practical scale reached by this approach. Its mathematical target remains the perturbed linear program, so the achievement should be understood in terms of that formulation rather than an unstated exact solution guarantee for the original problem.
icml-2020-eclipse-an-extreme-scale-linea.tldr: ECLIPSE uses distributed gradient optimization of a perturbed linear program's smooth dual to handle problems with one trillion decision variables.

paragraphs: Ordered Weighted L1 regression supports sparse learning with many features, but solving it can require substantial computation and memory. Standard proximal gradient methods repeatedly update parameters during optimization. This paper asks which updates can safely be avoided because the corresponding coefficients must be zero, reducing work without changing the result of the original algorithm.

The difficulty is that the regularizer couples coefficients through their ordering, so they cannot simply be handled independently. The proposed screening rule uses an iterative strategy to explore the ordering of the primal solution even though that structure is initially unknown. It then excludes parameters certified to have zero coefficients from further updates. The rule can be incorporated into both standard and stochastic proximal gradient methods.

The authors prove that algorithms equipped with the screening rule retain identical results to their original versions. Experiments across multiple datasets report significant computational gains without loss of accuracy relative to competitive algorithms. The key distinction is the certification behind the removal: computational savings come from avoiding updates that the optimization result does not need.
icml-2020-fast-oscar-and-owl-regression-.tldr: Safe screening accelerates OWL regression by skipping coefficients certified to be zero while preserving the original algorithms' results.

paragraphs: A recommendation system learns about unfamiliar options by suggesting them to users, creating a tension between gathering information and serving the current user. Users also have their own interests and need not follow recommendations. This paper studies whether useful exploration remains possible when the system must respect a strong duty to each user's expected welfare.

The authors formalize that duty through a constraint: the system may never recommend an action it knows has lower expected reward than the user would obtain by acting alone. This makes the user's independent choice the relevant benchmark. The restriction concerns expected reward and the system's knowledge, which are central to understanding what the proposed protection requires.

The main result is a recommendation algorithm that is asymptotically optimal, incentive compatible, and individually rational in an ex-ante sense. These properties combine long-run learning performance with incentives to follow recommendations and an advance expectation of acceptable participation. The positive result shows that exploration can coexist with the specified fiduciary constraint within the authors' model.
icml-2020-fiduciary-bandits-7bce273b24.tldr: The paper gives an asymptotically optimal recommendation algorithm that explores while respecting a formal constraint on each user's expected welfare.

paragraphs: Forecasting a sequence can benefit from accounting for the physical dynamics that generated it. The paper motivates its approach by observing that recurrent neural networks often overlook such structure. It develops a Consistent Koopman Autoencoder, drawing on Koopman-based methods for nonlinear dynamical systems to connect a learned forecasting model with an analysis of the underlying dynamics.

The distinguishing ingredient is the joint use of forward and backward dynamics. Rather than focusing only on how a system advances, the method also uses its backward behavior. The authors analyze the relationship between consistent dynamics and their associated Koopman operators, then directly connect the network design to that analysis. They report computational requirements comparable to those of the evaluated baselines.

Evaluation covers a broad range of high-dimensional problems with short-term dependencies. The method produces accurate estimates over substantial prediction horizons and exhibits robustness to noise in those evaluations. These findings suggest that incorporating consistency between the two directions of dynamics can be useful for forecasting, while keeping computation comparable to the alternatives considered.
icml-2020-forecasting-sequential-data-us.tldr: A Koopman autoencoder uses forward and backward dynamics to support accurate, noise-robust forecasting at computational cost comparable to evaluated baselines.

paragraphs: Frequency bias describes the tendency of networks trained by gradient descent to fit slowly varying patterns before rapidly varying ones. Prior explanations often consider uniformly distributed inputs, whereas real datasets can have uneven density. This paper uses the Neural Tangent Kernel model to investigate how local data density changes the dynamics of learning different frequencies.

Combining analytic and empirical observations, the authors report that learning a pure harmonic of frequency kappa at a point on the unit sphere takes time of order kappa to the power d divided by the local density. The relationship makes both frequency and sampling density relevant: within this setting, higher frequency and lower local density correspond to a larger convergence-time scale.

For inputs on the circle, the paper analytically derives the kernel eigenfunctions for two-layer networks. It also proves convergence results for deep fully connected networks using the kernel's spectral decomposition. Empirical comparisons identify similarities and differences between shallow and deep networks in this model, refining the picture of frequency bias beyond uniformly sampled inputs.
icml-2020-frequency-bias-in-neural-netwo.tldr: Neural Tangent Kernel analysis links the speed of learning harmonic functions to both their frequency and local input density.

paragraphs: Scheduling workloads across CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs requires accounting for differences among processors and their resource dependencies. Handcrafted scheduling heuristics often need to be developed separately for each application or system. Learning these heuristics with black-box methods can automate the search, but the required training data and training time can make that approach difficult to use.

Symphony introduces a Bayesian reinforcement learning model informed by the system architecture. Resource dependencies are built into the model, giving learning a domain-specific starting point. A second contribution is a sampling-based method for computing gradients of the Bayesian model without carrying out full probabilistic inference. The two techniques address the information needed for learning and the computational cost of the learning procedure.

The paper reports reductions in both training data and training time, alongside scheduling policies that outperform black-box approaches by up to 2.2 times. That figure is the reported upper extent of improvement, rather than a uniform gain. The findings support incorporating known system structure into the learning process for heterogeneous scheduling.
icml-2020-inductive-bias-driven-reinforc.tldr: Symphony combines architecture-informed Bayesian reinforcement learning with sampled gradients to reduce training demands and improve heterogeneous-cluster scheduling.

paragraphs: Kernel approximation represents a function using weighted kernel functions centered at selected locations. Choosing those locations and weights is central to interpolation and numerical integration, among other tasks. This paper studies the choice of locations for functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, introducing continuous volume sampling as a continuous counterpart of an existing discrete sampling distribution.

The main contribution is theoretical: the authors prove almost optimal bounds for interpolation and quadrature under this sampling scheme. The bounds apply to any Mercer kernel and depend on the spectrum of its associated integration operator. This gives a general route to guarantees that previously required specially designed node constructions for some particular function spaces.

The sampling distribution also has a useful computational property. Evaluating its probability density requires only pointwise kernel evaluations, unlike the requirements of the prior randomized approaches discussed in the paper. This makes the distribution naturally suited to Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers. The result combines broad approximation guarantees with a density that can be evaluated from direct access to the kernel.
icml-2020-kernel-interpolation-with-cont.tldr: Continuous volume sampling provides almost optimal kernel interpolation and quadrature bounds while requiring only kernel evaluations to compute its density.

paragraphs: A model can perform well on training and test data from the same source while relying on misleading shortcuts. A visual cue associated with one class may cease to be reliable when the association changes. This paper addresses that cross-bias generalization problem, where ordinary evaluation can conceal dependence on dataset-specific correlations.

The proposed framework deliberately constructs biased representations and encourages the desired representation to differ from them. The motivation is practical: specifying a representation that favors a shortcut can be easier than explicitly defining and measuring the bias itself. This provides an alternative to collecting or resampling data to break unwanted correlations, which can be costly or difficult.

Experiments spanning synthetic and real-world biases show that the method discourages shortcut use and improves generalization. The findings support using deliberately biased representations as a reference for learning less biased ones in the tested settings. The approach is particularly motivated by scenarios where those reference representations are easier to design than a complete description of the unwanted bias.
icml-2020-learning-de-biased-representat.tldr: Encouraging learned representations to differ from deliberately biased ones reduces shortcut reliance and improves generalization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies an Ising model whose graph structure changes over time but stays constant between change points. The learning problem has two connected parts: identifying when significant changes happen and recovering the graph within each stable interval. The number of change points is unknown, making it part of what must be inferred.

The method estimates each node's neighborhood by maximizing a penalized conditional log-likelihood. One part of the penalty promotes sparse graphs, favoring a limited set of connections. A fused-type penalty encourages the estimated structure to remain unchanged across stretches of time. Together, these penalties encode the desired combination of sparse relationships and piecewise constant evolution.

Under assumptions described as few, the authors establish two consistency theorems for change-point estimation. They identify these as the first such results for detecting an unknown number of changes in time-varying Ising models. Experiments on several synthetic datasets and one real-world dataset demonstrate the method's performance. The contribution combines a concrete estimation procedure with theoretical support for locating changes in the stated model.
icml-2020-learning-the-piece-wise-consta.tldr: Penalized neighborhood estimation jointly learns sparse Ising graphs and unknown change points, with consistency guarantees under stated assumptions.

paragraphs: A model-based reinforcement learning agent must learn enough about transitions to make good decisions. This paper studies finite-horizon episodes under the assumption that the true transition model belongs to a known model family. It evaluates learning through regret, the accumulated performance shortfall, and focuses model fitting on predictions that are directly connected to state values.

At each episode, the algorithm constructs a set of models consistent with collected data. Consistency is measured through squared errors in predicting state values along observed transitions, using the latest value estimate. The algorithm then plans optimistically over this set, choosing a new value function based on the promising possibilities still supported by the data.

For linear mixtures of d transition models, the regret bound is of order d times the square root of H cubed times T, up to logarithmic factors. Here H is the horizon and T the total interaction steps. The bound does not depend on the total number of states or actions. For general model families, the analysis instead uses Eluder dimension to characterize the learning difficulty.
icml-2020-model-based-reinforcement-lear.tldr: Value-targeted model fitting and optimistic planning yield regret guarantees independent of state and action counts for linear-mixture transition models.

paragraphs: Understanding a prediction can involve asking which group of training examples most influenced it. Influence functions approximate how removing training data would change the fitted model. Existing first-order methods can be inaccurate for groups because removing several examples may cause a substantial change in the optimal parameters, beyond what a first-order approximation captures well.

The paper proposes second-order influence functions for this group-level problem. The aim is to improve estimates of how a group's removal affects a particular test prediction. This shifts attention from the influence of isolated examples to the combined effect of a set, where the larger parameter change motivates a richer approximation.

For linear models, the authors examine groups of different sizes and types and report improved correlation between estimated influence and ground-truth influence. They also show that the second-order functions could be combined with optimization techniques to improve the selection of influential groups. The demonstrated improvement is specifically stated for linear models, while the broader motivation concerns explaining predictions through their training-data dependencies.
icml-2020-on-second-order-group-influenc.tldr: Second-order influence functions better estimate group influence for linear models and could improve searches for influential training groups.

paragraphs: Options provide reinforcement learning agents with behaviors that can help exploration and learning. This paper asks how to discover them before a particular reward function or task has been supplied. The approach uses the structure of the domain itself, allowing option discovery to proceed without knowing which outcomes a later task will reward.

The algorithm is derived from spectral graph theory and uses the full spectrum of the graph Laplacian. Its distinguishing choice is to include modes associated with higher graph frequencies, rather than following the more restricted spectral practice described for previous methods. These higher-frequency modes reveal subtleties of the domain that the paper shows can be useful when constructing options.

Geometric and manifold-based analysis provides a theoretical justification for the algorithm. Evaluations in several domains demonstrate clear improvements over competing methods. The combined message is that reward-free option discovery can benefit from a richer account of graph structure: details represented by higher frequencies can contribute useful information alongside the rest of the spectrum.
icml-2020-option-discovery-in-the-absenc.tldr: Using the full graph Laplacian spectrum enables reward-free option discovery that captures useful domain details and improves on evaluated alternatives.

paragraphs: Private query release aims to answer many statistical questions accurately while protecting the data used to answer them. This paper considers a setting with both public and private samples. Only the private samples must receive differential privacy protection, and the goal is to answer a specified class of queries with error at most alpha.

The research asks how many samples of each kind are needed. It develops upper bounds, describing achievable sample requirements, and lower bounds, identifying requirements that cannot generally be avoided. Treating public and private sample complexity separately makes it possible to characterize the information requirements of this mixed-data setting rather than considering all samples as interchangeable.

For private samples, the upper and lower bounds match in their dependence on the query class's dual VC-dimension, a measure of its complexity. For a large category of query classes, the public-sample bounds also match in their dependence on alpha. These are precise matches in particular dependencies, providing theoretical limits on the task without claiming that every component of the bounds coincides.
icml-2020-private-query-release-assisted.tldr: The paper establishes matching dependencies in sample-complexity bounds for differentially private statistical queries assisted by public data.

paragraphs: Self-play allows an agent to learn through competition with itself, but guarantees for learning against a fixed environment do not directly resolve the competitive case. This paper studies two-player Markov games, with particular attention to exploration and exploitation. Its performance criterion allows an adversarial opponent to exploit the agent's current strategy at any step.

The first algorithm, Value Iteration with Upper/Lower Confidence Bound, achieves regret growing as the square root of the total number of game steps, up to logarithmic factors. Measuring regret against a fully adversarial opponent makes the result relevant to vulnerability during learning, rather than only performance against a single fixed competitor.

A second algorithm separates exploration from exploitation. Its regret grows at the slightly worse rate of T to the two-thirds power, again up to logarithmic factors, but it has a worst-case polynomial running-time guarantee. The two results expose a tradeoff between the stated regret rate and the available computational guarantee. The authors present the work as, to their knowledge, the first line of provably sample-efficient self-play algorithms for competitive reinforcement learning.
icml-2020-provable-self-play-algorithms-.tldr: Two self-play algorithms provide regret guarantees against adversarial opponents, with a tradeoff between regret rate and worst-case computational guarantees.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning depends on gathering experience that improves a world model while also pursuing reward. Existing approaches can combine greedy policies with exploration heuristics or construct combined objectives in an ad hoc way. Ready Policy One frames this process as active learning: the agent should collect samples that improve its world model as efficiently as possible.

The framework uses a hybrid objective that adapts during optimization. This allows the balance between reward and exploration to change at different stages of learning. It also introduces a principled stopping mechanism for data collection, ending collection once the trajectory batch is sufficiently rich to improve the model. The method therefore addresses both which experience to seek and when enough has been gathered.

Evaluation on a variety of continuous control tasks shows statistically significant gains over existing approaches. These findings support the adaptive objective and collection framework in the evaluated tasks. The broader contribution is to make world-model improvement an explicit organizing goal for exploration, connecting the choice and quantity of collected experience to the learning process.
icml-2020-ready-policy-one-world-buildin.tldr: Ready Policy One adapts the reward-exploration balance and stops sample collection when trajectories are sufficient to improve its world model.

paragraphs: Automatically tuning an algorithm means choosing parameters based on performance on training instances. The practical question is how many instances are needed before that observed performance reliably represents expected future performance. This paper studies configuration problems where performance, viewed as a function of the parameters, can be approximated by a simpler function.

The crucial distinction is the type of approximation. When the approximation is uniformly accurate under the L-infinity norm, the authors obtain strong sample-complexity bounds. If accuracy holds only under an Lp norm with finite p, meaningful worst-case sample-complexity bounds are not possible on that basis. Thus, a uniformly controlled error offers a guarantee that an averaged error measure alone does not provide.

The authors evaluate their bounds in integer programming and obtain sample-complexity bounds up to 700 times smaller than previously best-known ones. This is an improvement in the theoretical training-set requirements evaluated there, rather than a claim of a corresponding runtime speedup. The work explains why the precise form of performance-function approximability matters when justifying parameter selection from data.
icml-2020-refined-bounds-for-algorithm-c.tldr: Uniform approximation enables strong algorithm-configuration sample bounds, while finite-Lp approximation alone cannot support meaningful bounds in the worst case.

paragraphs: Finding similar images or documents can use the Wasserstein distance, also known as an optimal transport distance. However, nearest-neighbor search under this measure becomes computationally demanding on massive datasets. This paper addresses that bottleneck by introducing Flowtree, an approximation algorithm for the Wasserstein-1 distance intended to combine fast computation with accurate similarity estimates.

The authors formally analyze both the approximation factor and the running time. These two aspects address different requirements: how the approximated distance relates to the target distance, and how much computation the algorithm needs. Studying them together gives a theoretical basis for using an approximation within nearest-neighbor search, where expensive distance comparisons can dominate the workload.

Extensive experiments evaluate Wasserstein-1 nearest-neighbor search on real-world data. Compared with the previous state of the art, Flowtree achieves running-time improvements of up to 7.4 times. This is the largest reported speedup rather than a promise for every search. The contribution combines analysis of the approximation with empirical evidence that it can substantially reduce the computational burden of this similarity measure.
icml-2020-scalable-nearest-neighbor-sear.tldr: Flowtree approximates Wasserstein-1 distance for nearest-neighbor search and reports speedups of up to 7.4 times over prior state of the art.

paragraphs: Sparse subspace clustering and spectral clustering both depend on relationships encoded in a data similarity matrix. This paper develops an explicit theoretical connection between them through that shared object. It shows that spectral clustering with a Gaussian kernel can be interpreted as sparse subspace clustering with an entropy-norm, which the authors call SSC+E.

Under this interpretation, SSC+E provides an analytical similarity matrix that is symmetric, nonnegative, and capable of nonlinear representation. It uses the Gaussian kernel to compute sparse similarities between objects, avoiding the complex sparse optimization program associated with conventional sparse subspace clustering. The connection therefore concerns both the mathematical meaning of the methods and the computation used to construct similarities.

The authors compare efficiency and effectiveness on ten benchmark datasets. Their theoretical and experimental analysis is intended to guide the choice of clustering algorithms for high-dimensional data. The abstract presents a relationship and a comparative study, rather than a universal ranking of the methods. Its main value is explaining how a familiar kernel construction fits within a subspace-clustering perspective.
icml-2020-sparse-subspace-clustering-wit.tldr: Gaussian-kernel spectral clustering can be viewed as entropy-norm sparse subspace clustering, connecting their similarity matrices and computational approaches.

paragraphs: Wasserstein losses compare probability distributions while accounting for geometry. Optimizing a sum of these losses can be expensive because existing techniques solve an optimization problem merely to obtain each gradient. Repeating that inner computation throughout a first-order method creates a substantial bottleneck. This paper develops an algorithm for a regularized version of the Wasserstein estimation problem.

The authors introduce a dual formulation that can be optimized with stochastic gradient steps computed directly from samples. Each step avoids an additional optimization problem, so estimation and computation proceed jointly. The time per step is sublinear in the problem's natural dimensions, addressing the cost of individual updates as well as the nested structure of the earlier computation.

The approach extends to other tasks, including Wasserstein barycenter estimation. The paper provides theoretical guarantees and illustrates performance using synthetic data. Its contribution is a way to reorganize regularized Wasserstein estimation around directly sampled updates, making repeated inner solves unnecessary for the proposed algorithm while retaining a theoretical account of its behavior.
icml-2020-stochastic-optimization-for-re.tldr: A stochastic dual method computes sample-based updates for regularized Wasserstein estimation without solving an extra optimization problem at each step.

paragraphs: Language understanding and language generation place different demands on a pretrained model. UniLMv2 combines autoencoding and partially autoregressive language modeling in one training procedure, called pseudo-masked language modeling. The two tasks train the unified model to serve as a bidirectional encoder and a sequence-to-sequence decoder, respectively, supporting both uses within the same pretraining framework.

Given text with hidden tokens, conventional masks teach relationships between the hidden content and its surrounding context. Pseudo masks support learning relationships within masked spans through partially autoregressive modeling. Carefully designed position embeddings and attention masks let the procedure reuse context encodings, avoiding redundant computation. Conventional masks also expose global masking information so that all position embeddings remain accessible in the partially autoregressive task.

Experiments report new state-of-the-art results across multiple widely used benchmarks covering language understanding and generation. These results support the effectiveness of the combined pretraining procedure in the evaluated tasks. The technical contribution is the coordination of complementary learning objectives and shared context computation within a single language model.
icml-2020-unilmv2-pseudo-masked-language.tldr: UniLMv2 combines autoencoding and partially autoregressive pretraining with reusable context encodings, reporting strong results in language understanding and generation.
